title: Lalit Modi Becomes a British Citizen, Leaving Extradition as India's Only Route Back
excerpt: The IPL founder announced the citizenship at the Oxford Union on November 14. Sources say it grants no immunity but closes the deportation route India tried in 2012.
body:
• Lalit Modi, the IPL founder who left India in 2010, announced at the Oxford Union on November 14 that he has become a British citizen. He said he celebrated the citizenship at a ceremony on September 15.
  • The change affects Modi personally only. It creates no new rule for other Indian nationals, visa holders or citizenship applicants.
  • Sources told The Times of India the citizenship gives him no legal immunity and does not formally stop extradition under the 1992 India-UK treaty, but it closes the deportation route and may have diminished the chances of his return.
  • Modi has repeatedly rejected the description of himself as a fugitive, arguing he has not been convicted of a crime. Indian agencies' allegations against him, which he disputes, remain under investigation.

Lalit Modi, the founder and former commissioner of the Indian Premier League, has announced that he has acquired British citizenship, nearly 16 years after he left India amid allegations of financial wrongdoing linked to his tenure running the league. Modi, 62, made the announcement while addressing the Oxford Union on November 14, and said in a post on X that he had celebrated the citizenship with family and friends at a ceremony on September 15, according to The Times of India and Mint reporting carried by TradingView.

"The United Kingdom has been my home for many years. It is a country I have come to admire and appreciate deeply — its people, institutions, traditions and values."

— Lalit Modi, announcing his British citizenship

Modi said becoming British was "a privilege and a responsibility that I embrace with pride, gratitude and a genuine sense of belonging," and signed off his announcement with "God Save the King," noting that he shared it on King Charles III's birthday.

What the citizenship changes — and what it does not

Sources told The Times of India that the citizenship does not grant Modi legal immunity and does not formally stop his extradition under the 1992 India-UK extradition treaty, but that it might have diminished, if not eliminated, the chances of his return, and that efforts to bring him back will continue. British nationality closes the door on deportation, leaving formal extradition as India's sole legal route, the sources said. The Times of India noted that UK citizens have previously been brought to India to face trial, citing AgustaWestland case accused Christian Michel and bookie Sanjeev Chawla.

India has been down the deportation route before. In November 2012, the UK government was formally requested to deport Modi to India, but the request was denied on December 21, 2012, citing domestic laws, The Times of India reported. The Enforcement Directorate had also sent a letter of request to the UK for execution of a non-bailable warrant against him.

The cases behind the standoff

Modi left India in May 2010, after the conclusion of the IPL's third season and his removal as IPL chairman by the Board of Control for Cricket in India. According to the Enforcement Directorate, as reported by The Times of India, Modi manipulated the process of assigning broadcast rights for the IPL in 2009, allegedly in exchange for a kickback of over Rs 125 crore. The ED's money laundering case followed an FIR registered against him by the Central Crime Branch of Tamil Nadu Police on October 13, 2010. The allegations also include bid rigging and violations of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, according to Madhyamam's report.

The ED had Modi's passport revoked by the Regional Passport Office in Mumbai on March 3, 2011; it was later restored on the directions of the Delhi High Court. In 2015, the CBI sent documents to Interpol seeking a notice against him, and a non-bailable warrant was issued against him in Mumbai. Modi has refused to return to India, citing threats from the underworld and other quarters, and has claimed he is the target of a political witch-hunt, which he says stalled the issuance of an Interpol Red Notice.

Earlier citizenship moves

This is not Modi's first change of nationality on paper. In 2025, he announced he was surrendering his Indian passport after acquiring citizenship in Vanuatu, a South Pacific island nation. Vanuatu's prime minister then ordered the cancellation of Modi's passport, stating it was an attempt to avoid extradition to India. The Times of India also reported that Modi had earlier applied for citizenship in the Caribbean nation of Saint Lucia through an investment scheme, after which the local Interpol unit there sought documents from India.

Modi has repeatedly rejected being labelled a fugitive, arguing that he has not been convicted of a crime and is not evading Indian authorities. In an interview with ANI earlier this year, he challenged investigators to prosecute him if there was evidence against him. What to watch now is whether India makes a formal extradition move under the 1992 treaty, and whether UK authorities take any step that changes his legal status.

nri_angle: The citizenship closes one legal route for a high-profile Indian case in the UK, a country home to a large Indian diaspora, while leaving the 1992 extradition treaty as India's remaining path.

Modi's passport was revoked by the Regional Passport Office.
UK denied India's request to deport Modi.
